claims.text: Overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by formation of a thermally stable nanocrystalline surface oxide layer.
The nanocrystalline oxide layer acts as a barrier to wear-induced damage and deformation.
Interactions between the oxide layer and substrate affect the coating's wear resistance.
Substrate thermal stability and degradation mechanisms contribute to the overall wear response.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating has a grain size of approximately 10–20 nm.
Tribological testing is to be performed at a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s and a normal load of 10 N.
Molecular-dynamics simulations are to use an EAM force field, a 1 fs time step, and a 10 ns simulation duration.
Testing across 25–400 °C in 25 °C increments can validate the proposed temperature-dependent wear mechanism.
The relevant structural mediator is a nanocrystalline oxide layer at the coating surface.
The modified high-temperature condition will produce a 30% increase in wear resistance relative to the room-temperature baseline.
The baseline coating exhibits a wear-volume loss of 10 mm³/m.
The proposed mechanism is applicable from 25 °C to 400 °C and from 10 N to 50 N.
Wear resistance may depend on substrate material, coating thickness, and testing conditions.
The proposed MD simulations may not fully capture oxide-layer–substrate interactions.
At temperatures above 200 °C, wear resistance should increase by at least 25% relative to the baseline if the hypothesis is correct.
